newsitem.title: USA: U.S. policymakers to confront air pollution debate.
newsitem.headline: U.S. policymakers to confront air pollution debate.

text.p: U.S. industry, electric utilities and the nation's air quality will be affected by three related issues that federal policymakers will grapple with next year.

Policymakers will decide whether to tighten standards against smog and airborne particles that damage lungs, whether to clamp tighter controls on industrial emissions that heat the earth's atmosphere, and how to restructure the electric power industry.

"The sources of the pollutants that make people sick and kill them from air pollution are the same sources that are making the planet sick from global warming. Two-thirds of the problem are power plants and cars and trucks," said Dan Becker, director of the Sierra Club's global warming and energy program.

The Environmental Protection Agency will decide in June whether it will impose tougher standards for smog and tiny airborne particles which it estimated will cost up to $8.5 billion a year in pollution controls to meet.
In international talks on global climate change, the United States has advocated setting legally binding commitments to reduce emissions from burning fossil fuels contribute to global warming.

And in a move that could help or hurt both of those efforts, Congress next year is to take up legislation that could lead to deregulation of the nation's electric power industry, a big source of air pollution.
The air quality standards and the global warming plan would set goals for reducing pollution, but at this stage would not dictate how they would be reached.

"The key is to have all those goals in front of us at the same time and then devise a strategy for achieving them simultaneously because if we don't do that then we'll make some very uneconomic investments," said Dan Lashof, a senior scientist with the Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC).

"We recognize that some of the strategies for any of these will have gains for the rest and we want to be very mindful of that as we move forward with implementation," an Environmental Protection Agency official said.
Most industries oppose the global warming and air standards initiatives, saying they would force expensive pollution controls on businesses and automobiles and would weaken the economy.

The White House has pushed tougher air regulations because it fears Congress would defeat a global warming treaty that forced big cuts in U.S. use of oil and other energy, Charles DiBona, president of the American Petroleum Institute, said.

"...they intend to go ahead with the global warming because the vice president (Al Gore) wants them to do it, but they can't get it though the Congress. So they are going to do it through regulations," DiBona said.
The plan for increasing competition in the monopolized and regulated electric power industry is a key to both global warming and the air quality issues, environmentalists say.
They want restructuring laws to lift exemptions that many older power plants have from Clean Air Act requirements.
They also want safeguards against utilities running their polluting coal-fired plants located mainly in the Midwest at full tilt to produce power to sell in other markets.
But electric utilities do not want the legislation that is supposed to increase their competitiveness to single them out for stricter pollution controls.

"If you are going to look at the environmental issues, you need to look at them in a holistic way, and not single out any particular participant in the marketplace," said David Owen, senior vice president at the Edison Electric Institute, which represents investor-owned utilities.

But several industry sources said clamping down on utilities will be easier to do politically than other measures such as making motorists use more expensive fuel instead of conventional gasoline, or requiring tighter pollution controls on factories, incinerators, and small businesses such as bakeries and dry cleaners.
